title: The Effect of Geometry on Thermodynamic Response
authors: Bojana Bokic, Sébastien R. Mouchet, Biljana Stankov, Sanja Ostojic, Nicolas Roy, Darko Vasiljevic, Yin Chang, Marija Radmilovic-Radjenovic, Branislav Radjenovic, Thierry Verbiest, Mohamed Hatifi, Branko Kolaric
abstract: At the nano- and microscale, various patterns influence and shape thermal and optical response, making them essential for the survival of various biological species. In addition, controlling thermal radiation is vital for a broad range of applications, such as thermal management, spectroscopy, optoelectronics, and energy conversion technologies. For this reason, there is strong pressure to elucidate the physics of thermal radiation at the nanoscale. In this article, we provide evidence that complex nanoscale geometries affect thermal management, leading to an unusual thermal response in heat-capacity measurements as a function of temperature. Beyond identifying the structural constraints associated with this unusual thermodynamic response, the current study introduces the possibility of shaping the apparent heat-capacity response through geometry without necessarily altering the system's chemistry.
summary: This work demonstrates that the intricate geometry of nanostructures, exemplified by insect elytra, profoundly dictates their thermal behavior. By analyzing heat capacity measurements and thermal imaging, the authors show that geometric features can induce anomalous thermodynamic responses, such as negative apparent heat capacity, through structural relaxation pathways. This highlights geometry as a primary control knob for thermal energy management at the nanoscale.
main_problem: The paper investigates how complex nanoscale geometries influence and shape the apparent thermodynamic response, particularly the heat-capacity, in materials like insect elytra.
main_result: Complex geometries can induce unusual, non-monotonic thermal responses, such as a decrease in apparent heat capacity, by modifying the energy barriers for internal relaxation mechanisms.
method: The study combines experimental measurements (DSC, thermal imaging) with theoretical modeling based on relaxation kinetics and geometric constraints.
model_or_system: The system studied is the nanostructure of insect elytra, modeled using thermodynamic principles that link chemical potential changes to surface curvature ($\Delta\mu \propto 1/R_1 + 1/R_2$).
key_observables: Apparent heat capacity ($C_{app}$), temperature profiles under laser irradiation, and the rate-dependent shift of the heat-capacity anomaly.
important_parameters: Curvature ($R_1, R_2$), temperature range (20°C to 140°C), and the activation energy barriers ($E_i$) governing relaxation.
main_assumptions: The unusual thermal response is attributed to geometry-driven internal relaxation mechanisms rather than bulk phase transitions, and the model uses a coarse-grained description of structural rearrangements.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the relationship between curvature and chemical potential, the experimental setup for thermal imaging, and the measured heat capacity curves showing non-monotonic behavior.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the importance of nanoscale geometry in thermal management, presenting experimental evidence from insect elytra using DSC and laser thermography, and concluding with a theoretical model linking geometry to the apparent heat capacity anomaly via relaxation kinetics.
why_interesting: The explicit mathematical linkage between geometric curvature (a classical structural parameter) and the thermodynamic response (heat capacity anomaly) provides a powerful, non-chemical mechanism for controlling energy storage and dissipation, relevant to understanding complex many-body systems.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Curvature influences the mutual interaction between a surface and its environment. The chemical potential is therefore modified: a positive curve (also referred to as anticline or convex surface) corresponds to a high chemical potential, whereas a negative curvature (also known as syncline or concave surface) corresponds to a low chemical potential.

Figure 2: The setup is designed to capture both direct and mirror-reflected thermal images in real time, allowing precise quantification of front and back temperature differences under laser irradiation: (left) setup in the laboratory during the experiment, (right) scheme of the setup (1 - FLIR camera; 2 - aluminum mount with the sample; 3 - laser pointer with a 532-nm wavelength; 4 - spherical mirror).

Figure 3: Species-specific surface patterns on the elytra of Morimus asper funereus (A) and Euchroma giganteum (B) reveal how geometry observed here by SEM may affect the thermal behavior. The heat capacity of the entire elytra of M. asper funereus (C) and E. giganteum exhibits minima as a function of the temperature (D). This is a behavior distinct from reported films and bulk materials [27–30]. The heat capacity of the black spots and the gray zone of M. asper funereus also differs from the curve corresponding to an entire elytron. Figures (B) and (C) were reproduced from ref. [36] and ref. [23], respectively.

Figure 4: Time-resolved thermal imaging reveals how laser irradiation generates distinct front–back temper- ature gradients across the elytron in four measurements on Morimus asper funereus. Average temperature of the outer (object) and inner (image) side of the elytra illuminated by a laser pointer at A) 405 nm, B) 650 nm. Maximum temperature of the outer (object) and inner (image) side of the elytra illuminated by a laser pointer at C) 405 nm, D) 650 nm. Here, "object" refers to the directly illuminated front side of the elytron, and "image" refers to the temperature of the back side as seen via reflection in the spherical mirror (Fig. 2).

Figure 5: The model predicts that sufficiently strong internal relaxation may drive the apparent heat- capacity signal below 0 J/g/K under certain conditions. Heating-rate dependence of the apparent heat- capacity anomaly predicted by the internal-relaxation model. The sample is driven through a temperature ramp T(t) = T0 + rt, while metastable internal states release stored enthalpy during the scan. Increasing the heating rate r shifts the capp p dip to higher temperature because the internal states have less time to relax at a given temperature.
